title: The Smile of Cold Spring
premise: Noor Vasquez returns to Cold Spring to bury his twin sister Nadia, whose body was identified by dental records that don't match her — they match Noor. The house he inherited hums with noises he has spent three years rationalizing, until the night his childhood imaginary friend, a boy called Wren, appears on the porch exactly as he looked in 1998, unchanged and unaging. Wren drags Noor into the house's buried history: in 1974, the previous owner, Alma Reyes, made a bargain with something beneath the spring to save her dying daughter, trading away a child's name and face — a debt that has passed down through every resident, now landing on Noor and the last living heir, elderly Miriam Hale, who is about to sign the property over to developers and sever the bargain's anchor forever. To survive, Noor must return what was taken in 1974 — give back the stolen name, the stolen face, the stolen years — which means surrendering either his own identity or the memory of everyone he loves, including Wren, who was never imaginary at all but the first child taken. In the end, Noor chooses truth over loyalty to his own survival: he speaks Alma's daughter's name aloud at the spring, releases Wren from his borrowed shape, and walks out of Cold Spring with no one left who remembers him — free, erased, and finally at peace.
about_author: Beatrix Reyes is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing estate sales in the Hudson Valley, where she collected the town legends that refused to stay filed. She writes horror about houses that keep receipts, and lives, deliberately, somewhere with no basement.

chapters.title: The Wrong Twin
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. At the funeral home, the mortician gently confirms the body's dental records belong to Noor, not Nadia. Noor signs anyway, telling himself it's clerical error. Emotional beat: grief curdling into denial as he drives to the house he inherited, refusing to look at his own reflection in the rearview.

chapters.title: Three Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, three days after moving in. Pipes knock in patterns; footsteps cross the attic above an unfinished floor. Noor narrates each noise with a rational cause, revealing how long this has been happening since Nadia's death. Beat: the exhausting discipline of disbelief.

chapters.title: Wren on the Porch
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. At dusk, a boy sits on the porch swing — Wren, the imaginary friend, unchanged since 1998, swinging his legs like no time passed. He says only: 'You came back to the wrong grave.' Beat: terror and a shameful flood of childhood comfort arriving together.

chapters.title: What Nadia Knew
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, searching Nadia's old room. He finds her notebooks: sketches of Wren, dates, and a page repeating 'the spring keeps what it's owed' alongside a photograph of the house dated 1974 with two girls out front. Beat: the realization Nadia wasn't running from grief — she was investigating.

chapters.title: Miriam Hale Signs Nothing Yet
chapters.summary: Noor visits Miriam Hale, 84, the last original resident, about to sell her land to developers. She recognizes him instantly — 'You have her face now, don't you?' — and slams the door. Beat: first confirmation that the wrongness is known, historical, and contagious.

chapters.title: The Spring Beneath
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, alien and patient. He leads Noor at night to the capped spring behind the properties, where the water moves against gravity. Wren explains nothing, only watches Noor's reflection ripple into someone else's. Beat: dread of a place that predates language.

chapters.title: Alma Reyes, 1974
chapters.summary: Interleaved: Alma's diary entries found in the crawlspace, read in Noor's voice. Her daughter drowned; something in the spring offered her back — for a name, a face, a childhood, payable down the generations. Beat: horror reframed as a mother's love weaponized.

chapters.title: The Face in the Casket
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. He exhumes the question literally: obtains the coroner's photos. The dead girl has his face — aged twenty-nine, drowned. Nadia's real body has never been found. Beat: loyalty to his sister's memory cracking against the truth that she may have traded herself.

chapters.title: Wren Was Real
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, in the county archive. A 1974 missing-child report: Wren Aldous, age nine, vanished near the spring — Alma's neighbor's son, the first payment. Every 'imaginary friend' in the family's history matches a missing child. Beat: the collapse of the boundary between imagination and appetite.

chapters.title: Nadia's Bargain
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, decoding Nadia's notebooks. Her final entry: she went to the spring to buy Noor back from a debt he'd unknowingly carried since childhood — the reason he survived the accident that should have killed him. Beat: love against duty, revealed as the family curse's engine.

chapters.title: The House Remembers Him
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The house begins erasing evidence of him: photos fading, his name peeling off mail, the funeral home calling about 'unclaimed remains.' The debt is collecting early because the sale will break its anchor. Beat: identity dissolving while he still breathes.

chapters.title: Miriam's Confession
chapters.summary: Miriam's POV. She was Alma's other daughter, the one who lived because someone else's name was given. She has kept the bargain fed for fifty years with small payments — memories, mostly — and begs Noor to stop the sale before everything unravels. Beat: complicity wearing the mask of kindness.

chapters.title: The Developer's Men
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Surveyors arrive at both properties; one goes pale at the spring and quits mid-shift, muttering that the water said his mother's maiden name. The sale accelerates. Beat: mundane greed colliding with ancient terms.

chapters.title: What Wren Wants
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, closest we come to his interior. He admits he led Nadia to the spring — the thing wears children's shapes to lure the next payer. But fifty years wearing Wren's shape has made something almost-human in him, and he wants, for once, to be returned rather than used. Beat: monstrousness and longing entangled.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Price
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Miriam offers him a way out: let the sale close, let the anchor break, and the debt dies with the land — but so does any chance of finding Nadia, and the released thing takes the town's memories of its dead with it. Beat: the theme crystallized — protect the lie, or tell the truth and lose everyone.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Signing day at the county office. Noor attends intending only to watch; instead he sees the buyer's lawyer carrying documents that include, inexplicably, a deed transfer for HIS house, dated 1974, signed in handwriting that becomes his own halfway across the page. Beat: the trap closing through paperwork.

chapters.title: Down to the Water
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, night before the sale finalizes. With Wren guiding and Miriam following with Alma's diary, they uncap the spring. The water rises to meet them, showing each of them the person they'd trade everything to see again. Beat: temptation staged as reunion.

chapters.title: Nadia, Underneath
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Nadia surfaces in the spring — alive, unchanged, three years drowned and breathing water. She begs him to take her place so the ledger balances and she can walk out. Beat: the cruelest test of love against duty, delivered by the thing wearing his sister perfectly.

chapters.title: The Name Returned
chapters.summary: Climax. Noor's POV. He refuses the trade and instead does what no payer ever tried: speaks Alma's drowned daughter's true name — recovered from the diary's marginalia — giving the debt back to its origin. The spring convulses; Wren sheds the borrowed boy-shape; Miriam collapses, fifty years of withheld grief flooding out. Beat: truth as exorcism.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Keeps
chapters.summary: Aftermath, Noor's POV. The spring goes still and ordinary. Nadia's body is found in the drained basin, three years dead after all — the vision was bait. Wren is gone, and with him every trace of the children the spring took, including their names from every record. Beat: victory that costs the dead their existence.

chapters.title: Erasure
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The price of speaking the name: the town's records of Noor Vasquez begin to thin — the funeral home has no file, Nadia's notebook pages about him blank. Only Miriam, holding his hand at the spring, remembers, and she is dying. Beat: chosen anonymity as both punishment and mercy.

chapters.title: The Smile of Cold Spring
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Miriam's POV in her last weeks, then a coda in Noor's. Miriam spends her remaining time writing Noor's story down so someone existed. Noor leaves town with a new name he chose himself, pausing at the property line where the spring runs clear and quiet — and smiles, genuinely, for the first time since he came home. Beat: peace purchased with selfhood, freely given.
